questions.q: What is the smallest positive integer n for which ((1 + i)/√2)ⁿ = 1?
questions.x: (1 + i)/√2 = cos 45° + i sin 45°, so by De Moivre's theorem its nth power is cos 45n° + i sin 45n°. This is 1 when 45n is a multiple of 360, first at n = 8. At n = 4 it is cos 180° = −1.

questions.q: Sets A and B satisfy A ∪ B = A ∩ B. What must be true?
o: A is a proper subset of B
questions.x: A ⊆ A ∪ B = A ∩ B ⊆ B, so A ⊆ B, and in the same way B ⊆ A. Hence A = B. Check with A = B = {1}: both sides are {1}; with B = ∅ and A = {1} the sides are {1} and ∅.

questions.q: A radioactive mass decays as m = m₀e^(−kt), with t in years. Half of it remains after 10 years. What is k?
questions.x: m₀e^(−10k) = m₀/2 gives e^(10k) = 2, so 10k = ln 2 and k = (ln 2)/10. Check: e^(−10·(ln 2)/10) = e^(−ln 2) = ½.

questions.q: lim(x→4) (x − 4)/(√x − 2) equals:
questions.x: x − 4 = (√x − 2)(√x + 2), so the fraction equals √x + 2 for x ≠ 4, which tends to 2 + 2 = 4. 1/4 is the limit of the reciprocal (√x − 2)/(x − 4).

questions.q: P and Q are square matrices of the same order. When is (P + Q)² = P² + 2PQ + Q²?
o: for every such P and Q
questions.x: (P + Q)² = P² + PQ + QP + Q², which equals P² + 2PQ + Q² exactly when QP = PQ. Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general, so it does not hold for every pair; P = Q is only one case where it holds.

questions.q: A system of linear equations that has at least one solution is called:
questions.x: A system with at least one solution (exactly one or infinitely many) is consistent; a system with no solution is inconsistent. Homogeneous means all the constant terms are zero.

questions.q: p is a real number. Which statement about the roots of x² + px − 4 = 0 is true?
o: They are real and equal for some real p
They are complex for some real p
They are real and distinct for every real p
They are real only when p ≥ 4
questions.x: The discriminant is p² − 4(1)(−4) = p² + 16, which is at least 16 for every real p. So it is never zero or negative and the roots are always real and distinct. A negative constant term with a positive x² coefficient always gives this.

questions.q: In the partial fractions of 6/((x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3)), what is the coefficient of 1/(x − 2)?
questions.x: Cover up x − 2 and put x = 2 in the rest: 6/((2 − 1)(2 − 3)) = 6/(−1) = −6. The full result is 3/(x − 1) − 6/(x − 2) + 3/(x − 3), and the three coefficients add to 0 as they must (no x² term on top). 3 is the coefficient of the other two fractions.

questions.q: What is the value of Σ (−1)ᵏ · k for k = 1 to 20?
questions.x: Pair the terms: (−1 + 2) + (−3 + 4) + … + (−19 + 20) is 10 pairs, each 1, so the sum is 10. Check: even terms sum to 110 and odd terms to 100, and 110 − 100 = 10. Starting with a + sign gives −10.

questions.q: Bilal has 3 shirts, 4 trousers and 2 pairs of shoes. One of the shirts does not go with 2 of the trousers. How many complete outfits (shirt, trousers, shoes) can he wear?
questions.x: Without the restriction there are 3 × 4 × 2 = 24 outfits. The banned ones are that shirt with either of the 2 trousers and any shoes: 1 × 2 × 2 = 4. So 24 − 4 = 20. Check directly: 2 × 4 × 2 + 1 × 2 × 2 = 16 + 4 = 20. Forgetting the shoes in the banned count gives 22.

questions.q: Three-letter codes are made from the 26 letters A to Z, and letters may repeat. How many codes contain at least one repeated letter?
questions.x: All codes: 26³ = 17576. Codes with three different letters: P(26, 3) = 26 × 25 × 24 = 15600. So 17576 − 15600 = 1976 have a repeat. Check: exactly two alike 3 × 26 × 25 = 1950, all three alike 26, total 1976.

questions.q: For every positive integer n, 1 + 2·2 + 3·2² + … + n·2^(n − 1) equals:
questions.x: For n = 2 the sum is 1 + 4 = 5 and for n = 3 it is 5 + 12 = 17; (n − 1)2ⁿ + 1 gives 5 and 17. Inductive step: (k − 1)2ᵏ + 1 + (k + 1)2ᵏ = 2k·2ᵏ + 1 = k·2^(k + 1) + 1. All four forms give 1 at n = 1, so checking n = 1 alone cannot decide.

questions.q: What is the value of sec 30° · cosec 60° + cot 45°?
questions.x: sec 30° = 2/√3 and cosec 60° = 2/√3, so their product is 4/3; adding cot 45° = 1 gives 7/3. Forgetting the cot 45° term leaves 4/3.

questions.q: With θ = 18°, 2θ = 90° − 3θ, so sin 2θ = cos 3θ. Using this, what is the exact value of sin 18°?
questions.x: 2 sin θ cos θ = 4 cos³θ − 3 cos θ; divide by cos θ: 2 sin θ = 1 − 4 sin²θ, so 4s² + 2s − 1 = 0 and s = (−1 + √5)/4 (positive root). (√5 + 1)/4 is cos 36°, and √(10 − 2√5)/4 is sin 36°.

questions.q: At what value of x does the graph of y = 2 sin(3x − π/2) reach its first maximum to the right of the y-axis?
questions.x: A maximum needs 3x − π/2 = π/2 + 2kπ, so x = π/3 + 2kπ/3; the smallest positive value is π/3. At x = π/6 the curve is at 0 and at x = 2π/3 it is at its minimum −2.

questions.q: A parallelogram has adjacent sides 6 cm and 10 cm, and one of its angles is 150°. What is its area in cm²?
questions.x: A diagonal splits it into two equal triangles, each of area ½ × 6 × 10 × sin 150° = 15, so the area is 30 cm². 15 is only one triangle, and 30√3 uses cos 30° instead of sin 150°.

questions.q: sin⁻¹(4/5) + sin⁻¹(5/13) equals:
questions.x: With sin A = 4/5 (cos A = 3/5) and sin B = 5/13 (cos B = 12/13), sin(A + B) = (4/5)(12/13) + (3/5)(5/13) = 48/65 + 15/65 = 63/65. Both angles are acute with A + B < π/2, so A + B = sin⁻¹(63/65); subtracting instead gives 33/65.

questions.q: The general solution of cos 2θ = cos²θ is (n ∈ Z):
questions.x: Write cos 2θ = 2cos²θ − 1: then cos²θ = 1, so cos θ = ±1 and θ = nπ. Check with cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ: the equation becomes sin²θ = 0, again θ = nπ. θ = 2nπ keeps only cos θ = 1.

questions.q: If y = √(x² + 9), what is dy/dx at x = 4?
questions.x: By the chain rule, dy/dx = 2x/(2√(x² + 9)) = x/√(x² + 9) = 4/5 at x = 4. Forgetting the inner factor 2x gives 1/(2×5) = 1/10; forgetting the ½ gives 8/5.

questions.q: What is the derivative of y = sin⁻¹(2x), |x| < 1/2?
questions.x: d/dx sin⁻¹u = u′/√(1 − u²) with u = 2x, giving 2/√(1 − 4x²). Missing the chain factor gives 1/√(1 − 4x²); 2/(1 + 4x²) is the derivative of tan⁻¹(2x).

questions.q: ∫ (ln x)² dx, for x > 0, equals:
questions.x: Parts with u = (ln x)², dv = dx: x(ln x)² − ∫2 ln x dx, and ∫ln x dx = x ln x − x, giving x(ln x)² − 2x ln x + 2x + C. (ln x)³/3 would be ∫(ln x)²/x dx.

questions.q: The area enclosed by the ellipse x²/9 + y²/4 = 1 is:
questions.x: The upper half is y = (2/3)√(9 − x²), so the area is 4 × (2/3)∫₀³ √(9 − x²) dx = (8/3)(9π/4) = 6π (the integral is a quarter circle of radius 3). This matches πab = π × 3 × 2; counting only the upper half (factor 2 instead of 4) gives 3π.

questions.q: Which differential equation has the family of parabolas y² = 4ax (a an arbitrary constant) as its solutions?
questions.x: Differentiate: 2y·dy/dx = 4a. Substitute for 4a: y² = 2xy·dy/dx, so y = 2x·dy/dx. Check with y = 2√(ax): dy/dx = √a/√x and 2x·dy/dx = 2√(ax) = y.

questions.q: After the axes are translated to a new origin O′, the point (3, −1) has new coordinates (5, 2). What is O′?
questions.x: With O′ = (h, k), x = X + h and y = Y + k: 3 = 5 + h and −1 = 2 + k, so O′ = (−2, −3). Check: (3 + 2, −1 + 3) = (5, 2). Subtracting the wrong way gives (2, 3).

questions.q: The lines represented by x² + 2hxy = 0 make an angle of 45° with each other. What is h?
questions.x: x² + 2hxy = x(x + 2hy) = 0: the y-axis and the line x + 2hy = 0 of slope −1/(2h). This makes 45° with the y-axis when the slope is ±1, so h = ±½. Check: tan θ = 2√(h² − ab)/|a + b| = 2|h| = 1.

questions.q: In a linear programming problem, what is the linear function that is to be maximised or minimised called?
questions.x: The function f = ax + by being optimised is the objective function. The inequalities are the constraints, and the points satisfying all of them form the feasible region.

questions.q: For the parabola y² = −8x, which statement is true?
o: Its focus is (−2, 0) and its directrix is x = 2
Its focus is (2, 0) and its directrix is x = −2
Its focus is (0, −2) and its directrix is y = 2
questions.x: y² = −4ax with a = 2: focus (−2, 0), directrix x = 2, opening to the left, latus rectum 4a = 8.

questions.q: A particle has position r(t) = t i + t² j. At what time are its velocity and acceleration perpendicular?
questions.x: v = i + 2tj and a = 2j, so v · a = 4t, which is zero only at t = 0. There the velocity i is along the x-axis and the acceleration 2j along the y-axis.

questions.q: What is the volume of the tetrahedron with vertices A(1, 1, 1), B(2, 1, 1), C(1, 2, 1) and D(1, 1, 3)?
questions.x: Edges from A: AB = i, AC = j, AD = 2k, with triple product 2. Volume = 2/6 = 1/3. Forgetting the 1/6 gives 2.

questions.q: A particle has displacement s = 6t² − t³ metres for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 s. What is its greatest velocity in this interval?
questions.x: v = 12t − 3t² and a = 12 − 6t = 0 at t = 2, where v = 24 − 12 = 12 m/s; this is a maximum since a changes from positive to negative. 32 m is the greatest displacement, at t = 4.

questions.q: h is Planck's constant and p a momentum. The quantity h/p has the dimensions of:
questions.x: h = [ML²T⁻¹] and p = [MLT⁻¹], so h/p = [L], a length (it is the de Broglie wavelength). Remembering h as energy × time can mislead students into answering time.

questions.q: A uniform rod 2 m long and of weight 40 N is pivoted at its lower end and held at 30° above the horizontal (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = √3/2). The torque of its weight about the pivot is:
questions.x: The weight acts at the centre, 1 m from the pivot along the rod; its moment arm is the horizontal distance 1 × cos 30° = √3/2 m, so τ = 40 × √3/2 = 20√3 N m. Using sin 30° gives 20 N m; using the full 2 m gives 40√3 N m.

questions.q: A cricketer catching a fast ball pulls his hands backward as he catches it. This reduces the force on his hands because it:
o: Reduces the change in the ball's momentum
Increases the time over which the ball's momentum is reduced to zero
Increases the impulse on the ball
questions.x: The change in momentum (the impulse) is fixed by the ball's mass and speed; spreading it over a longer time makes F = Δp/Δt smaller. The momentum change itself is not reduced.

questions.q: A ball is projected at 20 m s⁻¹ at 60° above the horizontal (cos 60° = 0.5). Ignoring air resistance, its speed at the highest point of its path is:
questions.x: At the top the vertical component is zero, leaving only the constant horizontal component: 20 cos 60° = 10 m s⁻¹. Saying zero confuses this with a ball thrown straight up; 10√3 m s⁻¹ uses sin 60°.

questions.q: The absolute gravitational potential energy of a body on the Earth's surface is −U₀. At a distance of 3R from the Earth's centre, where R is the Earth's radius, its absolute potential energy is:
questions.x: U = −GMm/r, so U ∝ 1/r: at r = 3R it is −U₀/3. Using 1/r² as for the force gives −U₀/9; reading 3R as a height above the surface (r = 4R) gives −U₀/4.

questions.q: A car of mass 1000 kg crosses the top of a hump-backed bridge, curved as a vertical circle of radius 20 m, at 10 m s⁻¹. The upward force of the road on the car at the top is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
questions.x: At the top the net downward force is the centripetal force: mg − N = mv²/r, so N = 10000 − 1000 × 100/20 = 10000 − 5000 = 5000 N. Adding mv²/r, as at the bottom of a dip, gives 15000 N; ignoring the circular motion gives 10000 N.

questions.q: A ceiling fan turns at a steady 300 revolutions per minute. Its angular velocity is:
questions.x: 300 rev min⁻¹ = 5 rev s⁻¹, and each revolution is 2π rad, so ω = 5 × 2π = 10π rad s⁻¹. Forgetting to divide by 60 gives 600π rad s⁻¹; taking one revolution as π rad gives 5π.

questions.q: When the speed of a liquid flowing through a pipe is increased beyond a certain critical value, the flow becomes:
o: Turbulent, with eddies and irregular paths
Steady, with streamlines fixed in place
questions.x: Below a critical speed the flow is laminar (streamline); above it the flow becomes turbulent, with eddies and irregular, changing paths. Speeding up a fluid does not remove its viscosity.

questions.q: A particle performs SHM of amplitude x₀. At what distance from the mean position is its speed half of its maximum speed?
questions.x: v = ω√(x₀² − x²) and v_max = ωx₀. Setting v = ωx₀/2 gives x₀² − x² = x₀²/4, so x = (√3/2)x₀ ≈ 0.87x₀. Assuming the speed falls linearly with distance gives x₀/2.

questions.q: Laplace's correction changes Newton's formula for the speed of sound in a gas by a factor of:
questions.x: Newton: v = √(P/ρ). Laplace replaced P by γP (adiabatic changes), so v = √(γP/ρ), larger by a factor √γ (about 1.18 for air). Multiplying the speed by γ itself forgets the square root.

questions.q: A stationary source emits sound of 400 Hz in still air, where sound travels at 320 m s⁻¹. An observer moves straight towards the source at 16 m s⁻¹. The wavelength of the sound around the observer and the frequency he hears are:
questions.x: The source is still, so the wavelength in the air is unchanged: λ = 320/400 = 0.80 m. The observer meets the waves at 320 + 16 = 336 m s⁻¹, so f′ = 336/0.80 = 420 Hz. Dividing 320 by 420 wrongly shortens the wavelength to 0.76 m.

questions.q: A photographer fits a polaroid filter to a camera and turns it to make a clear blue sky look darker. This works because:
o: The polaroid absorbs blue wavelengths only
Light scattered from the sky by the air is partly plane-polarised
Sunlight is completely polarised before it reaches the Earth
The polaroid lowers the frequency of skylight
questions.x: Sunlight scattered by air molecules is partly plane-polarised, so turning the polaroid to block that direction cuts the sky's brightness while light from clouds, which is unpolarised, is less affected. Direct sunlight is unpolarised.

questions.q: The core of an optical fibre has refractive index 1.60 and the cladding has refractive index 1.20. What is sin C, where C is the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary?
questions.x: sin C = n(cladding)/n(core) = 1.20/1.60 = 0.75. Using 1/n(core), as for a core in air, gives 0.625; dividing the other way gives 1.33, which no sine can equal.

questions.q: For an ideal gas, the molar specific heats at constant pressure and at constant volume are related by:
questions.x: For one mole at constant pressure, the extra heat beyond the constant-volume case does work pΔV = RΔT, so Cp − Cv = R.

questions.q: A certain amount of heat raises the temperature of a monatomic ideal gas by 30 K when the volume is kept constant. For this gas Cp/Cv = 5/3. If the same heat is given at constant pressure, the temperature rises by:
questions.x: Q = nCvΔT₁ = nCpΔT₂, so ΔT₂ = 30 × Cv/Cp = 30 × 3/5 = 18 K. It rises less, because part of the heat does work. Multiplying by 5/3 instead gives 50 K.

questions.q: A point charge sits at the centre of an imaginary sphere. If the radius of the sphere is doubled, the total electric flux through it:
questions.x: By Gauss's law Φ = q/ε₀, which depends only on the enclosed charge. The field falls as 1/r² while the area grows as r², so the product is unchanged.

questions.q: Three charges of +1 μC each are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 30 cm. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², what is the electric potential energy of the system?
questions.x: There are three pairs, each with U = kq²/r = 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻¹²/0.3 = 0.03 J, so U = 3 × 0.03 = 0.09 J. Counting one pair gives 0.03 J; counting only two gives 0.06 J.

questions.q: A potentiometer wire 2 m long of resistance 4 Ω is connected in series with a resistor R and a 2 V driver cell of negligible internal resistance. A thermocouple of emf 5 mV is balanced by 50 cm of the wire. The value of R is:
questions.x: Gradient = 5 mV / 0.5 m = 10 mV m⁻¹, so the 2 m wire has 20 mV across it and the current is 0.02/4 = 5 mA. The p.d. across R is 2 − 0.02 = 1.98 V, so R = 1.98/0.005 = 396 Ω. 400 Ω is the total circuit resistance, before subtracting the wire's 4 Ω.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's first rule (the junction rule: the total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it) is a consequence of the conservation of:
questions.x: Charge cannot pile up or disappear at a junction, so the current in equals the current out: conservation of charge. The loop rule is the one based on conservation of energy.

questions.q: A long solenoid is wound with 20 turns per centimetre and carries a current of 0.5 A. The magnetic field inside it is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
questions.x: n = 20 per cm = 2000 per m, so B = μ₀nI = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2000 × 0.5 = 4π × 10⁻⁴ T. Using n = 20 per metre gives 4π × 10⁻⁶ T.

questions.q: A power of 100 kW is sent along a transmission line of total resistance 5 Ω at a voltage of 10 kV. The power lost as heat in the line is:
questions.x: The line current is I = P/V = 100 000/10 000 = 10 A, so the loss is I²R = 100 × 5 = 500 W. At 1 kV the current would be 100 A and the loss 50 kW, which is why high voltages are used.

questions.q: A series RLC circuit is connected to an AC supply whose frequency is below the circuit's resonant frequency. Then:
o: XL is greater than XC, and the current leads the supply voltage
XC is greater than XL, and the current lags the supply voltage
XL equals XC, and the current is in phase with the voltage
XC is greater than XL, and the current leads the supply voltage
questions.x: Below resonance f is smaller, so XL = 2πfL is smaller and XC = 1/(2πfC) is larger. The circuit is capacitive overall and the current leads the voltage. Above resonance it is inductive and the current lags.

questions.q: In an electromagnetic wave travelling through a vacuum, the oscillating electric and magnetic fields are:
o: Parallel to each other and to the direction of travel
Perpendicular to each other but along the direction of travel
Perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
Parallel to each other and perpendicular to the direction of travel
questions.x: An electromagnetic wave is transverse: E and B oscillate at right angles to each other, and both at right angles to the direction in which the wave moves.

questions.q: A transistor with current gain β = 80 has a 2 kΩ resistor in its collector circuit. The base current increases by 50 μA. The increase in the voltage across the collector resistor is:
questions.x: ΔI_C = β ΔI_B = 80 × 50 μA = 4 mA, so ΔV = ΔI_C × R = 4 × 10⁻³ × 2000 = 8 V. Forgetting the gain gives 50 μA × 2 kΩ = 0.1 V; a prefix slip (2 kΩ taken as 200 Ω) gives 0.8 V.

questions.q: An ideal operational amplifier has an input resistance that is:
o: Infinitely large, so it draws no current from the input
Zero, so it draws a very large current
questions.x: An ideal op-amp has infinite input resistance, infinite open-loop gain and zero output resistance; the infinite input resistance means its inputs draw no current. This is why the current through the input resistor all flows through the feedback resistor.

questions.q: For an electron, h/m₀c = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m. The largest possible increase in wavelength of an X-ray photon Compton-scattered by a free electron is:
questions.x: Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ) is greatest at θ = 180°, where 1 − cos θ = 2, so Δλmax = 2 × 2.4 × 10⁻¹² = 4.8 × 10⁻¹² m. Taking θ = 90° gives 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m; zero shift happens at θ = 0°.

questions.q: In a target atom, the K-shell energy is −15.4 keV and the L-shell energy is −3.0 keV. The wavelength of its Kα X-ray line is about: (hc = 1.24 × 10⁻⁶ eV m)
questions.x: Kα is the jump from L to K: photon energy = 15.4 − 3.0 = 12.4 keV, so λ = hc/E = 1.24 × 10⁻⁶ / 12 400 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Using 15.4 keV alone gives 8.1 × 10⁻¹¹ m; adding the two energies (18.4 keV) gives 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ m; using 3.0 keV gives 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

questions.q: A piece of uranium-235 smaller than the critical mass cannot sustain a chain reaction because:
o: Its nuclei cannot undergo fission at all
Too many of the neutrons released escape from its surface before causing further fissions
It releases no neutrons when it undergoes fission
questions.x: In a small piece the surface is large compared with the volume, so many neutrons escape and, on average, fewer than one neutron per fission causes another fission. Each fission still releases 2-3 neutrons; the problem is losing them.

questions.q: The SI unit of the activity of a radioactive source, the becquerel (Bq), is equal to:
o: The activity of 1 g of radium
questions.x: 1 Bq = 1 disintegration per second. One joule per kilogram is the gray (absorbed dose), and the activity of 1 g of radium is the old unit, the curie.

questions.q: According to Hubble's law v = H₀d, with H₀ the Hubble constant, a rough estimate of the age of the universe is given by:
questions.x: If galaxies have been moving apart at steady speeds, a galaxy at distance d took time d/v = d/(H₀d) = 1/H₀ to get there, so 1/H₀ estimates the age. A larger H₀ would mean a younger universe.

questions.q: 4 g of methane is burned in a closed vessel with 32 g of oxygen: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Which reactant is in excess, and what mass of it is left over? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.x: CH₄ = 4/16 = 0.25 mol needs 0.5 mol O₂ (16 g). O₂ present = 32/32 = 1 mol, so 0.5 mol (16 g) of O₂ is left. Taking O₂ : CH₄ as 1 : 1 leaves 24 g; thinking CH₄ is in excess is the mass-not-moles slip.

questions.q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, when a gas is heated at constant pressure its volume increases because the molecules:
o: Move faster and strike the walls harder and more often, so the gas expands until the pressure falls back to its old value
Become larger in size when heated
Attract each other more strongly at higher temperature
Collide less often with the walls, because they move more slowly
questions.x: Higher temperature means greater average kinetic energy, so collisions become harder and more frequent; at constant pressure the gas expands until the collision rate per unit area falls back. The molecules themselves do not grow.

questions.q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, the actual volume of the gas molecules themselves, compared with the volume of the container, is:
questions.x: The theory treats gas molecules as points whose own volume is negligible compared with the space they move in; this is one of the two postulates that fail for real gases at high pressure.

questions.q: London (dispersion) forces between molecules arise from:
o: Hydrogen atoms bonded to N, O or F
Temporary dipoles that form in one molecule and induce dipoles in its neighbours
Transfer of electrons from one molecule to another
questions.x: Electron clouds shift for an instant, giving a temporary dipole that induces another in a neighbouring molecule; these forces exist between all molecules, even non-polar ones. Permanent dipoles give dipole–dipole forces instead.

questions.q: Electrons in a sample of hydrogen atoms are excited to the n = 4 level. When they return to the ground state, the maximum number of different spectral lines that can be emitted is:
questions.x: Possible jumps: 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1 and 2→1, i.e. n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6. Counting only direct jumps from n = 4 gives 3.

questions.q: The enthalpy change for CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g) is +1664 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the average bond energy of a C–H bond?
questions.x: Atomising one mole of CH₄ breaks four moles of C–H bonds, so the average is 1664 ÷ 4 = 416 kJ mol⁻¹. 1664 is the slip of forgetting there are four bonds; 333 comes from dividing by five atoms.

questions.q: The standard enthalpy of combustion of methane is −890 kJ mol⁻¹. What volume of methane, measured at STP, must be burnt to release 445 kJ of heat? (molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: Moles needed = 445 ÷ 890 = 0.50 mol, and 0.50 × 22.4 = 11.2 dm³. 44.8 dm³ comes from multiplying instead of dividing the energy ratio; 22.4 dm³ forgets the ratio altogether.

questions.q: Standard enthalpies of combustion: C₂H₄(g) −1411 kJ mol⁻¹ and C₂H₅OH(l) −1368 kJ mol⁻¹. Water does not burn. What is ΔH for C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(l) → C₂H₅OH(l)?
questions.x: Both sides burn to the same products (2CO₂ + 3H₂O), so by Hess's law ΔH = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products) = −1411 + 0 − (−1368) = −43 kJ mol⁻¹. +43 uses the formation-type rule (products minus reactants), which is wrong for combustion data; −2779 adds the two values.

questions.q: In the contact process, more air is used than is needed by the equation 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃. The effect of this excess oxygen is that:
o: A larger fraction of the SO₂ is converted to SO₃, because the equilibrium shifts to the right
The catalyst works only when oxygen is in excess
questions.x: Raising the concentration of a reactant (O₂) shifts the equilibrium to the right, so more of the costly SO₂ is converted. Kc depends only on temperature and does not change, which rules out the tempting 'Kc increases'.

questions.q: At 25 °C, the hydroxide ion concentration of a solution is 1 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. What is its hydrogen ion concentration? (Kw = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴)
questions.x: [H⁺] = Kw ÷ [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 10⁻³ = 10⁻¹¹ mol dm⁻³. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 10⁻¹⁷; 10⁻⁷ is the value for pure water.

questions.q: Which pair of liquids shows a positive deviation from Raoult's law?
questions.x: In ethanol–water the ethanol–water attractions are weaker than the hydrogen bonding in the pure liquids, so the vapour pressure is higher than predicted and a minimum-boiling azeotrope (about 95.6% ethanol) forms. Nitric acid–water and chloroform–acetone show negative deviation; hexane–heptane is nearly ideal.

questions.q: A cell has two copper electrodes, one in 0.010 mol dm⁻³ Cu²⁺ and the other in 1.0 mol dm⁻³ Cu²⁺, joined by a salt bridge. Using E = E° + (0.0591/n) log [Cu²⁺] for each electrode, what is the emf of the cell at 25 °C?
questions.x: The dilute electrode has E = E° + (0.0591/2)(−2) = E° − 0.0591 V; the other has E = E°. The difference is 0.0591 V. Taking n = 1 instead of 2 gives 0.118 V; the emf is not zero, because the concentrations differ.

questions.q: For a given reaction, the value of the rate constant k changes when:
o: The concentration of a reactant is doubled
The reaction mixture is diluted with solvent
The reaction has been running for some time
questions.x: k depends on temperature (and on a catalyst), not on concentration. Doubling or diluting a concentration changes the rate, but k stays the same; the falling rate during a reaction is also due to concentration, not to k.

questions.q: In a first-order reaction the reactant concentration falls from 0.80 mol dm⁻³ to 0.40 mol dm⁻³ in 20 minutes. How long does it take to fall from 0.40 mol dm⁻³ to 0.20 mol dm⁻³?
questions.x: The half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on the starting concentration, so each halving takes the same 20 minutes. 10 minutes would assume the half-life shrinks with concentration, as for a zero-order reaction.

questions.q: Mendeleev arranged the elements in his periodic table mainly in order of increasing:
questions.x: Mendeleev (1869) used atomic masses, as atomic numbers were not yet known. The modern table uses atomic number (Moseley), the usual mix-up.

questions.q: Which statement about the hydroxides of boron and aluminium is correct?
o: Both are amphoteric, because both elements are in Group IIIA
B(OH)₃ is basic but Al(OH)₃ is acidic, because aluminium is the larger atom
Both are strongly basic, because both elements lose three electrons
B(OH)₃ is acidic but Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric, because boron is smaller with a higher ionisation energy and is non-metallic
questions.x: Boron is a small, high-ionisation-energy non-metal, so B(OH)₃ behaves only as an acid; aluminium is more metallic, and Al(OH)₃ dissolves in both acids and alkalis. Assuming the same behaviour for the whole group is the tempting slip.

questions.q: Orthophosphoric acid heated strongly loses water to give metaphosphoric acid: H₃PO₄ → HPO₃ + H₂O. The oxidation state of phosphorus and the basicity of HPO₃ are:
questions.x: In HPO₃: +1 + x + 3(−2) = 0, so x = +5 (unchanged, since losing water is not redox); it has one O–H group, so it is monobasic. Keeping the basicity of the parent H₃PO₄ gives +5 and 3.

questions.q: Which halogen combines with hydrogen only slowly and reversibly, even when heated with a platinum catalyst?
questions.x: Reactivity with hydrogen falls down the group: F₂ explodes in the dark, Cl₂ explodes in sunlight, Br₂ needs heat, and I₂ + H₂ ⇌ 2HI is slow and incomplete because the H–I bond is weak. Bromine also needs heating but its reaction goes nearly to completion.

questions.q: In nickel tetracarbonyl, [Ni(CO)₄], the oxidation state of nickel and the geometry of the complex are:
questions.x: CO is a neutral ligand and the complex has no charge, so Ni is 0; four ligands around Ni(0) are arranged tetrahedrally. Taking the oxidation state equal to the number of ligands gives +4.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is:
questions.x: The longest chain has five carbons; numbering from the left puts the methyl groups on C-2 and C-3 (from the right they would be 3 and 4), so the name is 2,3-dimethylpentane. A branch named as ethyl or isopropyl means the longest chain was not chosen.

questions.q: Sodium ethynide, HC≡CNa, reacts with water to form ethyne and sodium hydroxide. This shows that:
o: Ethyne is a stronger acid than water
The ethynide ion is a weaker base than the hydroxide ion
Sodium ethynide is an oxidising agent
Water is a stronger acid than ethyne
questions.x: An acid–base reaction goes towards the weaker acid: H₂O gives H⁺ to HC≡C⁻, forming HC≡CH and OH⁻. So ethyne is the weaker acid and HC≡C⁻ the stronger base; reading the reaction backwards gives the tempting wrong option.

questions.q: 4-Methylbenzoic acid, CH₃C₆H₄COOH (–CH₃ and –COOH para to each other), is nitrated with concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄. The main product is:
o: An equal mixture of 4-methyl-2-nitrobenzoic acid and 4-methyl-3-nitrobenzoic acid
questions.x: –CH₃ (at C4) directs ortho to itself, to C3 and C5; –COOH (at C1) directs meta, also to C3 and C5. Both groups agree, so the nitro group goes to C3. Position 2 is ortho to –COOH and meta to –CH₃, favoured by neither group; the side chain is not nitrated under these conditions.

questions.q: Which group directs an incoming electrophile mainly to the ortho and para positions of a benzene ring?
questions.x: –OH has a lone pair on the oxygen next to the ring and donates electron density to the ortho and para positions. –CHO, –COOH and –SO₃H withdraw electrons and are meta directors.

questions.q: A mixture of 4.7 g phenol and 4.6 g ethanol is shaken with 1.0 mol dm⁻³ aqueous NaOH. What volume of the NaOH solution reacts with the mixture? (C₆H₅OH = 94, C₂H₅OH = 46 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: Only phenol is acidic enough to react with aqueous NaOH: 4.7/94 = 0.050 mol, needing 0.050 mol NaOH = 50 cm³. Including the 0.10 mol ethanol gives 150 cm³; using only the ethanol gives 100 cm³.

questions.q: A compound C₅H₁₀O gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, does not give a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent, and gives no yellow precipitate with iodine and NaOH. The compound is:
questions.x: 2,4-DNPH shows a C=O group; no silver mirror rules out the aldehyde pentanal, so it is a ketone. No iodoform rules out CH₃CO– ketones: pentan-2-one and 3-methylbutan-2-one, (CH₃)₂CHCOCH₃, both have it. CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ has none.

questions.q: Aldehydes and many methyl ketones form white crystalline addition products when shaken with a saturated aqueous solution of:
questions.x: The hydrogensulphite ion is a nucleophile that adds to the C=O carbon, giving a crystalline bisulphite compound. NaHCO₃ is the test for carboxylic acids, not carbonyl compounds.

questions.q: Which carboxylic acid also gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent?
questions.x: Methanoic acid, HCOOH, has an H on the carboxyl carbon, so it also behaves like an aldehyde and is oxidised to CO₂ and water, reducing Ag⁺ to silver. The other acids have no such H; choosing ethanoic acid confuses it with ethanal.

questions.q: Nylon-6, with repeat unit –NH(CH₂)₅CO–, can be made from a single monomer. That monomer is:
questions.x: The repeat unit holds one NH and one CO joined by five CH₂ groups, so one molecule carrying both an amino group and a carboxyl group, 6-aminohexanoic acid, condenses with itself. The diamine and the diacid together make nylon-6,6, the common mix-up.

questions.q: In the Solvay process for making soda ash, Na₂CO₃, the main raw materials are brine (NaCl) and limestone (CaCO₃). The main by-product is:
questions.x: Overall 2NaCl + CaCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂. Ammonia is recovered and reused, so NH₄Cl is only an intermediate; NaHCO₃ is the intermediate that is heated to give Na₂CO₃, and CaO is used up in recovering the ammonia.

questions.q: About what percentage of dry, unpolluted air by volume is nitrogen?
questions.x: Dry air is about 78% N₂ and 21% O₂, with about 1% argon and about 0.04% CO₂. Taking 21% confuses nitrogen with oxygen.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches a storage device with the way its data is read?
o: CD-ROM: a laser beam; hard disk: a magnetic read/write head
CD-ROM: a magnetic head; hard disk: a laser beam
CD-ROM: an electric charge in cells; hard disk: a laser beam
CD-ROM: a magnetic head; hard disk: an electric charge in cells
questions.x: Optical discs such as CD-ROMs are read by a laser that detects pits and lands; a hard disk is read by heads that sense magnetised spots. Electric charge in cells is how flash memory stores data, not either of these.

questions.q: When a computer is switched on, the first start-up instructions (such as the BIOS) are read from a memory that keeps them without power. This memory is:
questions.x: ROM is non-volatile and holds fixed start-up instructions that are needed every time the computer is turned on. RAM, cache and registers lose their contents when the power goes off.

questions.q: Which protocol does an e-mail program commonly use to download received messages from the mail server to the user's computer?
questions.x: POP3 (Post Office Protocol 3) collects incoming mail from the server to the client. SMTP is used to send mail towards a server, not to download received messages.

questions.q: In the term "IP address", what does IP stand for?
questions.x: IP is the Internet Protocol, which gives each device a logical address and carries packets across networks. A company that sells Internet connections is an Internet Service Provider, not IP.

questions.q: In which modulation is the frequency of the carrier wave changed according to the data, while its amplitude stays the same?
questions.x: Frequency modulation changes how often the carrier wave repeats, keeping its height constant. In amplitude modulation it is the height that changes and the frequency stays the same.

questions.q: A student quotes two short lines from a copyrighted book, with the book's name, in a review he writes for the school magazine. This limited use, generally allowed by law, is called:
questions.x: Fair use lets people use small parts of a copyrighted work for purposes such as review, teaching or criticism. It is not plagiarism because the source is named.

questions.q: Converting an encrypted, unreadable message back into its original readable form is called:
questions.x: Decryption turns ciphertext back into plaintext using the key. Encryption is the opposite step, turning plaintext into ciphertext.

questions.q: A user creates a new cloud server for herself from the provider's web page within minutes, without contacting any of the provider's staff. This cloud feature is:
questions.x: On-demand self-service means customers can set up resources themselves whenever they need them. Multi-cloud means using services from more than one provider.

questions.q: Machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with many layers, for example to recognise speech, is called:
questions.x: Deep learning is the branch of machine learning based on many-layered neural networks. An expert system works from rules given by human experts rather than learning layers from data.

questions.q: How is the root folder (top-level folder) of drive E written in Windows?
questions.x: A drive's root folder is written as the drive letter, a colon and a backslash, `E:\`. All other folders on the drive are inside it, such as `E:\Notes`.

questions.q: Cell A1 holds 150. What does the formula `=A1*20%` show?
questions.x: 20% means 0.2, so 150 × 0.2 = 30. 3000 would come from multiplying by 20 instead of 20%.

questions.q: In which data model are the data and the procedures that act on the data stored together as objects?
questions.x: The object-oriented model stores objects that combine attributes (data) and methods (procedures). The relational model stores data only, in tables.

questions.q: A college replaces its separate Admissions, Library and Accounts files with one shared database in which each student's address is stored only once. What is the direct benefit?
o: Every office keeps its own copy of the address for safety
Programs must be rewritten whenever a field is added
Records can be read only in the order they were stored
A change of address is made once and every office sees the same address
questions.x: Storing the address once removes redundancy, so one update keeps the data consistent for all offices. Keeping separate copies in each office is exactly the file-system problem the database removes.

questions.q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
In Access, the criteria `Between 400 And 600` is typed under Price. How many records does the query return?
questions.x: Between includes both end values, so 450, 600, 500 and 400 match: 4 records. Only 700 and 350 are outside the range; leaving out the two end values would give 2.

questions.q: Which Access action query copies the records it selects into a brand-new table?
questions.x: A make-table query creates a new table from the query's result. An append query adds the selected records to a table that already exists.

questions.q: Which preprocessor line is written correctly?
questions.x: A directive starts with #, the word include is in lower case because C is case-sensitive, and a standard header's name goes in angle brackets, not round ones. Without the angle brackets or the #, the line is an error.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
printf("a\\nb");
```
o: a and b on two separate lines
questions.x: \\ is the escape sequence for one backslash, so the characters printed are a, \, n, b: a\nb on one line. There is no \n escape here, so no new line is started.

questions.q: Which keyword declares a variable for a floating-point number with double precision?
questions.x: double gives about twice the precision of float. long and int are integer types and cannot hold fractions.
a is printed before it is updated: the values of a are 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 over the 6 passes (each new b is the sum of the old a and b). 1 1 2 3 5 8 would print b instead of a.

questions.q: In the call `area(5, 3)`, the values 5 and 3 are called the:
questions.x: Values written in a call are the actual arguments; they are copied into the formal parameters named in the function's header. The return value is what comes back, not what is sent.

Inside main the local t (10) hides the global t. inc() changes only the global t (4 -> 5 -> 6); main prints its own local t, which is still 10. 6 is the global value, which main cannot see by that name.

questions.q: In the Waterfall model, the documents produced in the design stage are mainly used as the input to which stage?
questions.x: Each Waterfall stage feeds the next: programmers write the code from the design (flowcharts, data structures, screen layouts). Requirements analysis and the feasibility study come before design, not after it.

questions.q: Classes Car and Bus are written as `class Car(Vehicle):` and `class Bus(Vehicle):`. Both use the attribute `wheels` and the method `start()` that are written only once, in Vehicle. Which OOP feature does this show?
questions.x: Car and Bus are child classes that receive Vehicle's attribute and method without rewriting them: inheritance. Polymorphism would need the same method name to behave differently in each class.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
x = 9
x //= 2
x **= 2
print(x)
```
questions.x: `x //= 2` floor-divides: 9 // 2 = 4. Then `x **= 2` squares it: 16. 20.25 would come from true division (4.5 squared).

questions.q:
What happens when this code runs?
```
class Player:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
p = Player()
print(p.name)
```
o: a TypeError, because no value is given for `name`
questions.x: `__init__` needs a `name` argument besides `self`, but `Player()` passes none, so creating the object raises a TypeError and nothing is printed. Python does not fill a missing parameter with None.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
print(len({"x": 1, "y": 2, "z": 3}))
```
questions.x: `len` of a dictionary counts its key: value pairs, and there are 3. 6 wrongly counts the keys and values separately.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
L = [7, 4, 9, 2, 8]
m = 0
for i in range(1, len(L)):
    if L[i] < L[m]:
        m = i
L[0], L[m] = L[m], L[0]
print(L)
```
questions.x: The loop finds the index of the smallest value, m = 3 (the value 2), and the last line swaps it with L[0]: [2, 4, 9, 7, 8]. This is one selection-sort pass, so the list is not fully sorted.

questions.q: Ali, Bina and Hamid join an empty queue at a bank counter, in that order. One customer is served, then Dawood joins, then two customers are served. Who is now in the queue?
questions.x: A queue serves first in, first out: Ali leaves first; Dawood joins at the rear behind Bina and Hamid; Bina and Hamid are served next, leaving Dawood. "Ali only" is what a stack (last in, first out) would leave.

questions.q: A bar chart shows two shops' sales of 92 and 96 units, but its vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0, so one bar looks three times as tall as the other. What is wrong with the chart?
o: It exaggerates a small difference and can mislead readers
It should be a pie chart, because there are only two values
Nothing; the axis may start at any value without changing the picture
The two bars should be in the same colour
questions.x: With the axis starting at 90 the bars show 2 and 6, so a 4-unit gap (about 4%) looks like a threefold difference. Starting a bar chart's axis at 0 keeps the bar heights in proportion.

questions.q: When judging an online source, which criterion asks how recently the information was published or updated?
questions.x: Currency is about the date: whether the information is up to date. Authority asks who wrote it and whether they are qualified.

questions.q: What is the main point of the passage?
o: Village seed banks keep local varieties whose qualities may one day be needed
Farmers should stop buying modern seed from shops
Old local varieties always give heavier yields
Seed banks need large buildings to work well
questions.x: The passage describes village seed banks and says "they keep choices open" for a year "of drought or a new disease". Giving up modern seed is wrong: the banks "are no argument against modern seed".

questions.q: According to the passage, how is the stock of a village seed bank kept fresh?
o: The seed is sealed in tins and never opened
New seed is bought from shops every year
Farmers borrow seed and return more after the harvest
Old seed is thrown away after one season
questions.x: "A farmer may borrow a few kilograms at sowing time and return a larger amount after the harvest, so the stock is renewed". Sealed tins are mentioned, but only as containers.

questions.q: The passage suggests that a local variety is most likely to be lost when:
o: it is stored in a labelled clay pot
a drought shows how valuable it is
farmers stop resowing it because a higher-yielding seed is easy to buy
a family lends some of it to a neighbour
questions.x: Local varieties survived because they were "saved and resown by families over generations"; they are disappearing now that seed "comes from a shop" with "heavier yields". Storing seed in a pot is how the banks keep it, not how it is lost.

questions.q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "traits" most nearly means:
questions.x: The "traits" are then listed: surviving frost, ripening on little rain, being ignored by pests, all qualities of a crop. Habits of character is the meaning used for people, not plants.

questions.q: The writer's attitude towards modern shop-bought seed is best described as:
o: accepting of its benefits while warning of what is being lost
questions.x: The writer grants that new varieties "often give heavier yields" but says "something has been lost in the change". Hostility is wrong: the banks "are no argument against modern seed".

questions.q: The passage mainly argues that:
o: money already spent and lost should not decide what we do next
film tickets should never be bought in advance
people should give up any project that runs into difficulty
companies are better than families at managing money
questions.x: Economists warn that a sunk cost "should play no part in decisions about the future", and the writer asks "is the next rupee worth spending?" Giving up at any difficulty is rejected in the last paragraph.

questions.q: Why, according to the passage, does a company keep putting money into a failing project?
o: A new project would cost it more over a year
Economists have advised it to keep going
Stopping would mean admitting that its earlier spending was a mistake
The project is close to success
questions.x: The company carries on "because abandoning it would mean admitting that the earlier spending was a mistake". The cost "over a year" belongs to the family's car, not the company.

questions.q: Which of these decisions would the writer consider sensible?
o: A shopper keeps using a faulty phone because she paid a lot for it
A family keeps repairing an old car because of what they have already spent
A man finishes a dull book only because he bought it
A student leaves a paid course when he sees its remaining classes will not help him
questions.x: The student judges the course "by what lies ahead", as the writer advises; the other three act on money already spent, the very "trap" described. Leaving is not giving up "at the first difficulty", since he has judged the rest useless.

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "abandoning" most nearly means:
questions.x: The company keeps paying because stopping the project would mean admitting a mistake, so "abandoning" it means giving it up. Starting again is close to the opposite.

questions.q: The writer's attitude towards people who fall into the trap described is best described as:
o: understanding, though still convinced they are mistaken
indifferent, giving no view about them
questions.x: The writer says "The trap is understandable" but that past spending is "a reason for regret, not a reason to continue". The writer never mocks them, only notes that "no one likes to look foolish".
